newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine war turns into a battle for investments.
newsitem.headline: Philippine war turns into a battle for investments.

text.p: Philippine Moslem rebel leader Nur Misuari was proclaimed head of a semi-autonomous regional government on Friday, clearing the way for a new offensive -- the battle to secure vital investment to make his peace deal with the government work.

"We are here determined to prove to the people that we are going to sustain the momentum of peace," Misuari, a former university political science teacher, said after his proclamation at Election Commission headquarters in Manila.
"And we are going to use that peace as the sine qua non for economic development, economic progress and ultimately economic prosperity for our people," he said.
Misuari, chairman of the Moro National Liberation Front, was the only candidate for the governorship of the Autonomous Region of Moslem Mindanao (ARMM) in Monday's elections.
The ARMM, set up in 1990, covers four Moslem-majority provinces in the southern Philippines and has limited autonomy.
Misuari, who had previously refused to have anything to do with the ARMM, ran for election as governor after agreeing to a peace pact with the central government of President Fidel Ramos.
The main thrust of the peace plan involves setting up a Southern Philippines Council for Peace and Development that Misuari will also head.
The council will oversee development projects in 14 southern provinces, although it will have no political powers and will report directly to Ramos.
The peace deal envisages the council as a precursor to an expanded autonomous area, which the 14 southern provinces will decide whether to join by referendum in three years.
Accepting the governorship of the ARMM gives Misuari a chance to demonstrate his administrative abilities and to reassure Christians who have opposed the peace pact.
Misuari and Ramos travel together on Saturday to Butuan on Mindanao island to attend a business conference aimed at drumming up investment for the region.
Both have said that the success of their peace agreement, which ended 24 years of war that killed about 120,000 people, depends on economic growth in the south, long the country's poorest region.
So far, neither the government nor Misuari have outlined specific business plans.
Misuari said the ARMM elections had proved that the MNLF was committed to peace.
"No one now could dispute the fact that our recently concluded election was the most peaceful ever in the annals of Philippine politics," he told reporters.
He said that previous elections in the south had been notorious for their violence, with rival political supporters using heavy machineguns and even mortars.
This time, he said, there had been no bloodshed.
